66119.etyen:
Borrowed from Middle Low German wafel (“waffle; waffle iron”), whose basic meaning referred to a cake or baking iron patterned like a honeycomb. The Middle Low German word is possibly derived from Old High German wabo (“honeycomb”) or waba, and is related to veve (“to weave”), German weben, Dutch weven and English weave. The probable semantic development was “woven or interlaced structure” → “honeycomb or honeycomb pattern” → “patterned baking iron” → “the cake baked in it”.
The needlework sense is a shortening of vaffelsøm (“waffle stitch”), while the carpet-underlay sense is a shortening of  / Borrowed from German Waffel (“blow to the mouth”), from a dialectal sense whose original meaning was “large, hanging mouth”, related to dialectal German Waffe (“large mouth”) and waffen, wafen (“to talk, howl”), probably ultimately onomatopoeic. It is historically separate from Etymology 1, although the two words have probably often been associated with one another.
First attested in 1834 in the expression en varm vaffel (“a hard slap; a box on the ear”).
Compare Dutch wafel (“blow to the mouth, slap”).

From Latin aberrāns (“wandering, straying or deviating from”), present active participle of aberrō (“to wander, stray; aberr”), from both ab- (“from, away from”), from ab (“from, away from, of”), from Proto-Italic *ab, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”) + and from errō (“to wander, astray; err”). 1000263.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Italian ciao (“hello; goodbye”), from Venetan s-ciao (“servant, slave”) or sciavo (“servant, slave”), especially in the expression s-ciao vostro, literally “your slave”, used in the sense “at your service; your humble servant”. The Venetan word is from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), from Ancient Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos, “Slav”), from earlier Σκλαβηνός (Sklabēnós, “Slav”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *slověninъ (“Slav”). The deeper origin of the Proto-Slavic ethnonym is uncertain.

1005127.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂éd
Compound of g-moll (“G minor”) + akkord (“chord”), literally “G-minor chord”.
The first element g-moll (“G minor”) contains the musical note name g (“G”) and moll (“minor”). The latter is via German Moll (“minor”) from Middle High German bēmolle (“B-flat; soft B”), from Medieval Latin b molle (“soft B”). The adjective is from Latin mollis (“soft, mild”), from Proto-Italic *moldus (“soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dús (“soft, weak”), from the root *(s)meld- (“to soften, melt”).
